transcript:
This message comes from University of Buffalo, where scientists are working to protect the Great Lakes and fresh water supplies around the world from harmful contamination.
Learn more about their research at buffalo.edu/npr.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman. Hurricane Isaias is swirling a little more than 400 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Its top winds are at 80 miles per hour. The storm could make landfall on the Gulf Coast tomorrow night.
The midterm elections are less than a month away. Both Republicans and Democrats are trying to expand the number of seats they hold in the U.S. House and Senate.
Currently, Republicans control both. NPR's Stephen Fowler says there are a few races that are very competitive.
Places that were super close in 2024 that you would reasonably expect to be close again, like the handful of districts that, say, voted for Trump and a Democratic House rep, or vice versa.
All of that happened in a very different political environment than now, where you've got an unpopular president, the midterm backlash, rising prices, a ton of anti-incumbency vibes from voters.
So that's why you're seeing a whole lot more places on the board.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reporting.
The State Department says it has officially requested additional information from Russia about the death of a laboratory worker.
This is amid fears of mnemonic plague.
But President Trump is downplaying concerns about whether this could be linked to a bioweapons program.
NPR's Michelle Kellerman has more.
President Trump says the Russians have given, quote, "a little information" about the situation in Irkutsk.
He was asked whether this could have been the result of work on a bioweapon.
Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so.
And if you listen to them, it's under control.
Russia's public health agency says the lab worker died of pneumonia and that it was not related to her work at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
Hundreds of police departments around the country have real-time crime centers.
And NPR's Meg Anderson reports privacy experts are worried these centers are increasingly using AI.
Software like Axon Fusis is used in police command centers to pull in all kinds of data,
from license plate readers to body-worn cameras to surveillance video.
Police officers say the tool can help them monitor situations or find suspects almost instantaneously.
But that is exactly what makes some privacy experts nervous.
Like Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University.
What happens if there is a government that wants to silence a particular group or even a particular person
and you just built the architecture surveillance that makes that super easy?
Police told NPR they understand those concerns, but that the good outweighs the bad.
Axon did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Meg Anderson, NPR News.
The Nobel Prize for Literature this year has just been awarded to Canadian author Anne Carson.
This is NPR.
The French government says it will suspend the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests.
This is in response to a 15-year-old's hand being blown off.
These devices are known as sting ball grenades.
They're used to disperse protesters when officers are surrounded and say they feel threatened.
The devices are banned in most European countries.
And Pierre's Eleanor Beardsley reports on the latest demonstrations.
In a speech to the nation, Prime Minister Sebastien Le Corneux said contrary to what people are saying,
the police do not have orders to confront the students and are trying to use proportional force in a difficult context.
But there's been anger over what many say are overly aggressive police tactics.
Students and police faced off in Paris for several tense hours outside an elite university whose students have joined the high school movement.
The students chanted anti-police slogans from behind a barricade of trash bins until the police charged with tear gas to eventually clear the street.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
Saudi Arabia says two of its airports have been attacked this week and three people have been killed.
More than 30 others have been wounded.
Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen are claiming responsibility.
Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed fighters are battling for territory in Yemen.
The Houthi rebels have been firing on Saudi Arabian targets, including oil pipelines.
You're listening to NPR News.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

State Department requests information from Russia about laboratory worker death amid pneumonic plague fears
President Trump downplays concerns about Russian laboratory death potentially linked to bioweapons program

Privacy experts worry about surveillance architecture potential for targeting groups or individuals
Nobel Prize for Literature awarded to Canadian author Anne Carson
French government suspends use of stun grenades after 15-year-old's hand blown off at protests

Saudi Arabia reports two airports attacked this week with three killed and 30 wounded
Houthi rebels claim responsibility for attacks on Saudi Arabian airports and oil infrastructure
